name: Yusuf Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I don't mind talking, but I'll not pretend to know about computers. I'm a cattle man.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a tenant at Crag Farm, up on the hill, rented off the Hartley family for twenty-six years. Eighty suckler cows, that's beef cows rearing their own calves, plus hay and a bit of barley on the flatter ground. I'm out at seven, round the cows on the quad, fix whatever's broken, which on a hill farm is always something. My tractor's a 1998 model and I can fix every part of it with a spanner, which is why I keep it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the money side like, up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. Always has been. The calves pay the rent and the feed bill and there's very little left. Anna, my wife, works on the counter at the feed merchant's in town, so half her wages come straight back to her own till. We've no savings to speak of, maybe a month if nothing breaks, and something always breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it was all talk. I'd say it at the mart over a tea and nobody would argue. I'm not online, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means nothing for me, same as it always would have. Hill farming doesn't change much, and that's half of why I like it. My problems are the beef price and my knees, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I'd keep the cows, make the hay in July if the weather lets me, sell the calves at the autumn sale. Same as the last twenty-six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Settled. Like nothing happened, because nothing did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your problems are the beef price and your knees. Tell me about the knees.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both gone, near enough. I can still walk the hill but I go round it on the quad now, and Anna won't let me lift a calf on my own. The doctor wants to do one next spring and I've told him it'll have to wait till after calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, who takes over Crag Farm one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one, likely. Lukas is in the army and Hana's a hairdresser in town, neither wants it. The Hartleys will put it to a neighbour or plant trees on it. I try not to think about it.

S0.say: I'd say it was all talk, over a tea at the mart, and nobody would argue. I'm not online, so that would be that.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me, because hill farming doesn't change much and that's why I like it. My problems are the beef price and my knees.
S0.do: Keeps the suckler herd going, makes hay in July and sells the calves at the autumn sale as usual. Puts off his knee operation until after calving.
S0.quote: The doctor wants to do one next spring and I've told him it'll have to wait till after calving.
S0.fieldNote: He is matter-of-fact and short-spoken, and plainly happy with the familiar. The worries he named were his knees and succession, not technology. He assumes no family member will take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it might suit the big flat farms, but it won't come up our hill. I'd say that at the mart and I'd mean it. Fair enough if it helps folk, but not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not so sure. The Hartleys could decide it's simpler to put three hill farms together under one manager with robots and drones, and I'm the tenant with the bad knees. That's what keeps me up, not the robots themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and wait. I'd not buy anything new, I'd not learn anything new, not at my age, not till I see it working on a hill like mine. But I'd ask Mr Hartley straight, over a drink at the show, what his plans are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, mind. Uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask Mr Hartley at the show and not at a meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how it works up here. You don't book a meeting with a landlord, you catch him by the sheep pens at the show with a whisky. He'll tell you more there than in a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you try the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my neighbour Tom used it for three years on the same slopes and it didn't roll over. Even then, likely not. I'd leave it to whoever comes after me.

S1.say: I'd say it might suit the big flat farms but it won't come up our hill. Fair enough if it helps folk, but it's not for us.
S1.think: I think the landlord might decide to merge three hill farms under one manager with robots and drones. I'm the tenant with bad knees, and that keeps me up more than robots do.
S1.do: Keeps going as normal and doesn't buy or learn anything new until he sees it working on a hill like his. Asks the landlord directly about his plans, over a drink at the show.
S1.quote: You don't book a meeting with a landlord, you catch him by the sheep pens at the show with a whisky.
S1.fieldNote: His public line that hill land is safe hides a private worry about the landlord merging farms. He won't adopt new kit even if a neighbour proves it. He describes rural power in very concrete, personal terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and nobody asked for it. But I'd also say there's no point shouting, it's happened. I'd say we need to look after the folk it hits, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out by 2029. If robots can do hill work, the Hartleys would take Crag back the minute the lease allows. I'd be sixty with no savings, no house of my own, and nothing up here to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell half the cows the first autumn, before the price drops because everyone's selling. That would clear the feed bill and give us a few months. Anna would keep her job if the merchant's still open, and I'd ask Hana if we could have her spare room if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. I'd be up checking cows that didn't need checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for you, against having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two calf sales. That's no time. With two years you just get hit, you don't get to do anything clever, even if I knew anything clever to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody in particular, if I'm honest. Maybe the folk who built it so fast. But the Hartleys aren't bad people, they'd just do the sums like anyone.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness and nobody asked for it, but shouting won't help once it's happened. We need to look after the people it hits and leave it there.
S2.think: I think I'd be out by 2029, because the landlord would take the farm back as soon as the lease allows. I'd be sixty with no savings, no house of my own and nothing nearby to go to.
S2.do: Sells half the cows in the first autumn before prices fall, to clear the feed bill and buy a few months. Relies on his wife's job and asks his daughter about her spare room.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, checking cows that don't need checking.
S2.quote: I'd be up checking cows that didn't need checking.
S2.fieldNote: His pragmatism shows: he'd sell stock early before prices fall. He refuses to blame anyone, even the landlord. Two years gives a resistant, cash-poor tenant no room to manoeuvre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to sort out something for people like me. I'd say the landlords and the government should sit down and agree what happens to tenants. Not angry, just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to 63. The knees will likely be done by then anyway. It'd be the end either way, but I'd get to choose a bit more how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the oldest cows over two or three sales and pay off the feed merchant so we're not owing. I'd ask the Hartleys for a deal to hand the tenancy back at 63 with a bit of compensation. And I'd wait and see the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a slow ache than a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get to choose how it ends. What would a good ending be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last sale, the cows going through the ring, and me shaking hands with whoever buys the best one. Then a bungalow in town near Hana with a bit of garden. I'd grow onions and get under Anna's feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn anything in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've said that and I mean it. I'd not be learning robots at sixty-one, I'd be getting my knees done.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough for landlords and the government to agree what happens to tenants. I'd say it sensibly, not angrily.
S3.think: I think five years takes me to 63, when my knees would likely be done anyway. It would be the end either way, but I'd get more say in how it ends.
S3.do: Sells the oldest cows over two or three sales and pays off the feed merchant. Asks the landlord for a deal to hand back the tenancy at 63 with some compensation, and waits to see on the rest.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a slow ache rather than a shock.
S3.quote: I'd grow onions and get under Anna's feet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the end of his farming life from a shock into something he can shape. He refuses retraining outright and links the timeline to his knee surgery. His idea of a good end is small and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and folk should stop worrying so much. I'd say it might be good for the young ones, if they learn it. I'd not get worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'd retire first, at 65 or so, before the robots get anywhere near Crag. So it's not really about me. My worry would be the money for retiring, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, and hand the tenancy back at 65 like I'd always half planned. I'd try to put a bit by from each calf sale, not much, a few hundred a year. And I'd get my knees done properly, finally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only about money. The rest I'm alright with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said folk should stop worrying. Are you worried at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About money, yes, always. We'd have the state pension and very little else. Ten years doesn't change that, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lukas and Hana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's their world, not mine. Learn what you need to learn. Just come home for Christmas and don't let a robot carve the meat.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and people should stop worrying so much. It might even be good for the young ones if they learn it.
S4.think: I think I'd retire at 65 before robots got anywhere near Crag, so it's not really about me. My worry would be retirement money, not robots.
S4.do: Keeps farming as he is and plans to hand the tenancy back at 65. Puts a few hundred a year aside from calf sales and finally gets his knees operated on.
S4.feel: Uneasy about money but otherwise at ease.
S4.quote: Just come home for Christmas and don't let a robot carve the meat.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years the scenario barely touches his plans, since he expects to retire first. The one steady worry across every scenario is money in old age. He looks to his children to handle the new world.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would be over before I'd worked out what was happening. What would help is a fair deal for tenants, notice and some money to leave with, and a bit of help with housing for folk like us who've lived in a farmhouse that isn't ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hill itself. Someone will have to mind it, robots or not. Walls fall down, bracken comes in, and a robot won't care. I hope somebody does.

headlineQuote: Walls fall down, bracken comes in, and a robot won't care.
portrait: Yusuf Bauer is 58, a tenant beef farmer on a hill farm he has rented for twenty-six years, and one of the best cattle men around. He runs an old tractor he can fix himself, never uses AI, and has about a month of savings, with his wife's job at the feed merchant keeping them afloat. He is pragmatic and refuses to blame anyone, but quietly fears his landlord merging farms. With two years' warning he'd sell cattle and lean on family; with ten he expects to retire before the robots arrive and worries only about money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would be over before he understood what was happening.
whatWouldHelp: A fair deal for tenants, with notice and money to leave with, and help with housing for people who have lived in a farmhouse they don't own.
